overview: This file documents the wartime transmission to the U.S. Department of State of a League of Nations Drug Control Service study of narcotics and opium smoking in Japanese-ruled Taiwan (Formosa). Two substantially duplicate copies of the study describe the applicable international conventions and colonial ordinances; the Government General’s regulation of manufacture, trade, prescribing, addiction, and illicit traffic; coca cultivation and cocaine production; the government opium monopoly; the licensing, rationing, surveillance, and compulsory treatment of smokers; and detailed production, consumption, stock, trade, enforcement, and revenue statistics. A covering embassy despatch and a personal letter from Bertil A. Renborg explain the report’s transmission to George A. Morlock, while later annotations and a State Department form record its declassification in 1950.

subfiles.title: League of Nations note on narcotics and opium smoking in Formosa, duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Drug Control Service, League of Nations Secretariat
subfiles.about: A comprehensive study of narcotic-drug regulation, production, trade, addiction, and the government-controlled opium-smoking system in Japanese-ruled Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The note outlines the international conventions and colonial ordinances governing narcotics in Formosa and identifies the Police Bureau of the Government General at Taihoku as the central control authority. It describes coca cultivation, cocaine manufacture, the production of crude morphine as a by-product of prepared opium, and the licensing and inspection of manufacturers, dealers, pharmacists, and smokers. Extensive tables cover estimated requirements, consumption, imports, exports, stocks, seizures, smoker numbers, and monopoly revenue. The second part reconstructs the history and operation of the opium monopoly, including rationing, police surveillance, dross destruction, compulsory cures, penalties, and smuggling through Taiwanese ports.

subfiles.title: Declassification annotation for duplicate of Despatch No. 19704
subfiles.from: Jane A. Davis, DC/R; W. Walter Anderson, Chief, Records
subfiles.about: An archival annotation records the authority and approval for declassifying a duplicate enclosure to the London embassy despatch.
subfiles.summary: The annotation identifies the item as a duplicate of the enclosure to Despatch No. 19704 of December 6, 1944, filed under 894A.114 Narcotics/12-6-44. It records declassification approval on August 21, 1950, and refers to the attached DS-507 form for authority.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 19704 transmitting a note on narcotics in Formosa
subfiles.from: John M. Allison, for the U.S. Ambassador, American Embassy, London
subfiles.about: The American Embassy forwards Renborg’s League of Nations study for transmission to George A. Morlock of the Far Eastern Division.
subfiles.summary: John M. Allison encloses a note prepared by Bertil A. Renborg of the League of Nations Drug Control Service on narcotic drugs, opium smoking, and the drug situation in Formosa. He asks that it be transmitted to George A. Morlock in the Department of State’s Far Eastern Division.

subfiles.title: Letter from Bertil A. Renborg to George A. Morlock
subfiles.about: Renborg sends his Formosa drug-control note and reports progress on a companion study of Japan proper.
subfiles.summary: Renborg encloses his note on drug control in Formosa and expresses the hope that it will be useful. He acknowledges Morlock’s November 10 letter and the accompanying Japanese legislative texts, explaining that they require revision of his draft note on Japan proper, which he expects to send the following week.

subfiles.title: Enclosure: Control of narcotic drugs and opium smoking in Formosa
subfiles.from: Drug Control Service, League of Nations Secretariat
subfiles.about: The classified enclosure provides the League of Nations’ detailed account of narcotic control and the opium monopoly in Japanese colonial Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: This enclosure is another version of the November 25 League study, based on Japanese legislation and reports supplied to international drug-control bodies. It surveys regulation, manufacture, coca cultivation, cocaine and morphine production, legitimate consumption, international trade, policing, penalties, and illicit markets. Its second part traces the licensing of smokers from 1900 onward and explains monopoly sales, individual rations, household inspections, compulsory treatment, port smuggling, prosecutions, and government revenue. Several pages are duplicated within the surviving file, providing parallel readings of some tables and passages.

subfiles.title: Request for declassification of Despatch No. 19704 and enclosure
subfiles.to: State Department originating or action division
subfiles.about: Form DS-507 requests and records the declassification of the confidential enclosure on narcotics in Formosa.
subfiles.summary: The form identifies Despatch No. 19704, sent by the American Embassy in London on December 6, 1944, and its subject, “Transmitting note on narcotics in Formosa.” It records a decision to change the enclosure’s classification from confidential to unclassified, citing a June 6, 1950 memorandum from Mr. Kotschnig and showing final records approval on August 21, 1950.

interest: The file offers an unusually detailed quantitative and administrative portrait of how Japan governed narcotics in colonial Taiwan, including the striking coexistence of declared prohibition with a profitable state monopoly that licensed, rationed, and closely surveilled chronic opium smokers. It is also valuable for the history of coca and cocaine production, since the report identifies Formosa as one of the world’s few coca-growing centers and documents its manufacturing and export system. The correspondence reveals wartime transfer of League of Nations expertise to American officials concerned with East Asia, while the duplicate report copies permit comparison and correction of damaged or inconsistent readings. The 1950 annotations additionally preserve a compact record of the State Department’s postwar declassification process.
